vignette:
Clinical PTSD Case Vignette (66-year-old Female, Shopowner)

She first describes herself as "a woman who used to laugh a lot." That feels like a different life now-before the morning that changed everything. She remembers the date exactly, because it was her shop's ten-year anniversary. She had set out a small table of pastries near the door, a quiet celebration for regulars. Around 9 a.m., a police officer entered, not in uniform, but he flashed a badge and asked about a disturbance the night before. She didn't understand-nothing had happened. She told him so, politely. He became insistent, then loud. Another officer came in. Within minutes, she was shoved backward into her own shelves, her wrist twisted as they handcuffed her in front of two customers. They accused her of harboring a man from a nearby protest. She had no idea who they meant. She was released after an hour, but the physical pain and humiliation did not leave.

That was four years ago. Now, the shop feels smaller, darker. She keeps the blinds half-closed, even on bright days. Every time a police car passes on the main street outside her storefront, she flinches and freezes mid-motion-hand hovering over the cash register, breath held until the engine fades. Customers have noticed; some have stopped coming. She tells herself it's fine, that her shop was never really thriving anyway, but the truth is she avoids serving anyone in a blue uniform. Last month, a delivery driver in a navy polo shirt bent over to sign a receipt, and she dropped a stack of invoices, her hands trembling so badly she couldn't pick them up. She mumbled an excuse about low blood sugar and retreated to the back room.

At night, the memories come. She wakes at 2 a.m., reliving the crack of her shoulder hitting the metal shelf, the sound of her own voice saying "please, please," while the officer's face was inches from hers, his voice cold. She has not told her ex-husband-they have been divorced for eleven years, and she rarely speaks to him. Her adult children live in another region; she texts them cheerful emojis and avoids calls because she cannot fake a steady voice. She has stopped attending the monthly community meetings she once organized. The thought of being in a crowded room with a uniformed security guard at the door makes her stomach clench.

She used to walk to the park every Sunday. Now she drives three blocks to a different grocery store because the one near the park has a police substation attached. She does not say "trauma." She says, "I'm just getting old, and I'm tired." But her body remembers differently: a racing pulse when she hears a sudden shout outside her shop, a cold sweat when a stranger knocks on the locked back door. She has started leaving the shop exactly at 5 p.m., even if she has not finished inventory. She cannot stay in the building after dusk.

Her PCL-5 score is 78, but she does not know that number. She only knows that she has not laughed in a long time. She sits in my office-referred by her primary care doctor for "anxiety"-with her hands clasped tightly in her lap, wearing a floral blouse that seems too cheerful for the weight she carries. She looks past me toward the window the entire hour. After a long silence, she says, "I used to think I was strong. Now I just want to be small."
